ety.text: From Middle English onyoun, oynoun, from Old French oignon, from Latin ūniōnem, accusative of ūniō (“onion”), which had also been borrowed into Old English as yne, ynnelēac (“onion”) (> Middle English hynne-leac, henne-leac). Displaced the inherited term ramsons. * (soy): Stems from a 4chan word filter which changes the word soy to onions. The word filter was implemented in relation to the "alpha onion eater" meme, which is depicted as the direct opposite of the soy boy.

senses.d: A monocotyledonous plant (Allium cepa), allied to garlic, used as vegetable and spice.
ex: Some of the weeds that cause an undesirable flavor in milk are: onion, tarweed, scaleweed, garlic, mustard, pepper grass.

senses.d: The bulb of such a plant.
ex: My eyes are stinging from the chopped onions.
Among the ancient Greeks, onions are most frequently mentioned as a stimulus to sexual desire.

senses.d: Any of various plants, mostly of the genus Allium, that are more or less similar to Allium cepa.
Soy, particularly when used in compound words related to the soy boy stereotype.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French oingnon, from Old French oignon, from Latin ūniōnem.
Inherited from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.
Inherited from Old Spanish cebolla, from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa (whence English chive via French). Compare Galician and Portuguese cebola, Catalan ceba, and Asturian cebolla.
